title: Your raga
hook: after a whole block of moods, some listeners find one raga that feels like home, and a line in Sri Rag's var says what makes a raga worth it

segments.voice: Yesterday, raga kirtan today: ragis and teachers who still sing each shabad in its named raga. Your line was the old tunes live. Who taught you something by ear? Day one thousand one hundred thirty.

Some people come alive before sunrise, with the kettle and the dark window. Others are only themselves after dinner, with the lamps on. Some love a heavy morning that has work in it; some wait all year for spring. Nobody chose this exactly. It just turned out to be home. We've walked through the ragas of the Guru Granth Sahib for weeks, one mood after another. Some listeners, at the end of a road like that, find that one of them has quietly become theirs. Today: your raga.
screen: `WHICH HOUR IS YOURS?` → `ONE MOOD AFTER ANOTHER.` → `ONE THAT FEELS LIKE HOME.`

segments.voice: Lay out a few of the rooms we've stood in. Kedara at dusk, tender as the light goes. Bhairao, the serious morning, opening with nothing happens outside you. Basant, where spring is always present. Kalyan in the evening, with a bee that comes back again and again. Prabhati at daybreak, with the Name as an ornament. Jaijavanti, where the ragas end: remember; this is your work. Each one put a mood around the same Word. Now, a line from the Granth itself about ragas. In the var of Sri Rag, Guru Amar Das writes, in paraphrase: among the ragas, Sri Rag stands high, if through it one comes to love the True One. Hear the condition at the end. If. The raga's worth isn't in the notes alone. It's in what the singing does to the heart. A raga that leaves you cold hasn't done its work for you yet, however fine it is. A raga that turns you toward the One has. That makes 'my raga' a modest claim. It isn't saying this raga is better than the others. It's saying: this is where, for now, the love arrives most easily for me. Tradition gives ragas their hours and seasons, and the hymns inside them say what they say. But the listener is part of the music too. Your hour of the day, your season, the mood you live in most often, these may lead you to one raga before the rest. And the Granth's line suggests the test: not which one sounds best, but which one leaves you nearer. Today's line: my raga.
screen: `DUSK, MORNING, SPRING, EVENING, DAWN.` · `SRI RAG STANDS HIGH, IF.` · `THE WORTH IS IN THE LOVE.` · `NOT THE BEST: THE NEAREST.` · then, large: `MY RAGA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name your raga. Sit, and let the ragas we've met pass by slowly in your mind: the dusk one, the serious morning, spring, evening, dawn, the last raga. Don't judge them. Just notice which one your breath settles into. If none does, that's fine; notice which hour of the day feels most like home, and let that be your guide for now. When one rises, say its name once, silently. If you pray, you can hold it the way Guru Amar Das's line suggests, as a way toward love of the True One. If you don't, simply let the name be a small marker of where you feel at home. The bell holds the time.
Your raga. The one mood of the Granth's music where, for now, you come nearest; Guru Amar Das says a raga is worth it if through it one comes to love the True One. Today's word.
Your line: my raga. Today, at your favorite hour, play one shabad in the raga you named, or simply sit for a minute in that hour and let it be yours. Day one thousand one hundred thirty.

howItsDone: Listeners of kirtan often come to love particular ragas and particular ragis; in the gurdwara, the raga sung usually follows the hymn's heading and the time of day.
